t: True or false? Participation in community life is one of the fundamental principles of British life.
e: Participation in community life is one of the five fundamental principles of British life, alongside democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and tolerance. The handbook encourages everyone to get involved, for example by volunteering or helping in local groups.

t: True or false? You can take the Life in the UK test at any college or school.
e: You cannot take the test at any college or school. It must be taken at a registered and approved Life in the UK test centre, booked online.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Everyone living in the UK is expected to respect and obey the law.
Only British citizens are expected to obey the law.
e: Everyone living in the UK, not just citizens, is expected to respect and obey the law. This is one of the responsibilities of living in the UK.

t: Besides passing the Life in the UK test, what else is usually needed to apply for settlement or citizenship?
o: Evidence of English speaking and listening at B1 level or above
A British sponsor for every year of residence
e: To apply for settlement or citizenship you usually need to pass the Life in the UK test and show you can speak and listen in English at B1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference, or above. A degree, sponsor or driving licence is not required.

t: True or false? People on work visas normally must pass the Life in the UK test to become permanent residents.
e: The Life in the UK test is usually taken by people who want to become permanent residents or citizens, including those who came on work visas. They must also show their English language ability.

t: What do you need to apply for settlement in the UK? (Choose TWO)
o: A pass in the Life in the UK test
Evidence of English speaking and listening at B1 level
e: To apply for settlement you usually need to pass the Life in the UK test and show evidence of English speaking and listening at B1 level or above. A driving licence or British spouse is not required.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Tolerance of those with different faiths is a fundamental principle of British life.
Following the state religion is a fundamental principle of British life.
e: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is a fundamental principle of British life. There is no requirement to follow any state religion.

t: Where can you book the Life in the UK test?
o: By phone to the Home Office
e: You can only book the Life in the UK test online, at an approved test centre. There are about 60 test centres around the UK.

t: In which part of the world is the UK located?
e: The UK is located in the north-west of Europe. The longest distance on the mainland is from John O'Groats in Scotland to Land's End in England, about 870 miles.

t: Which TWO countries have devolved parliaments or assemblies?
e: Scotland has a Parliament and Wales an Assembly, each with devolved powers; Northern Ireland also has an Assembly. England does not have its own devolved parliament, and the Isle of Man is not part of the UK.

t: Which TWO of these are part of the United Kingdom?
e: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are Crown dependencies with their own governments and are not part of the UK.

t: Which part of the island of Ireland is an independent country?
o: The rest of Ireland outside Northern Ireland
e: The island of Ireland is divided. Northern Ireland, in the north-east, is part of the UK. The rest of the island is the Republic of Ireland, an independent country.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Isle of Man has its own government.
The Isle of Man is governed directly by the Scottish Parliament.
e: The Isle of Man is a Crown dependency with its own government. It is not part of the UK and is not governed by the Scottish Parliament.

t: True or false? British overseas territories such as St Helena are part of the UK.
e: British overseas territories, such as St Helena and the Falkland Islands, have strong links with the UK but are not part of it.

t: Which Dylan Thomas poem was written for his dying father?
o: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night
e: Dylan Thomas wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night' for his dying father. His radio play Under Milk Wood is also very well known.

t: Frank Whittle, who developed the jet engine, was a member of which service?
e: Sir Frank Whittle, a British Royal Air Force engineer officer, developed the jet engine in 1930.

t: What were "pocket boroughs"?
o: Constituencies controlled by a single wealthy family
e: In the 18th century, some constituencies were controlled by a single wealthy family; these were called 'pocket boroughs'. Constituencies with hardly any voters were called 'rotten boroughs'. Both were abolished by the Reform Act of 1832.

t: Which TWO things did the Romans bring to Britain?
e: The Romans built roads and public buildings, created a structure of law, and introduced new plants and animals. The English language came from the Anglo-Saxons, and the printing press much later, with Caxton.

t: In what year did the English Civil War begin?
e: The English Civil War between Charles I and Parliament began in 1642. The king's supporters were called Cavaliers and Parliament's supporters Roundheads.

t: Skara Brae, the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe, is on which islands?
e: Skara Brae, on Orkney off the north coast of Scotland, is the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe. It helps archaeologists understand how people lived near the end of the Stone Age.

t: Which TWO did Richard Arkwright develop?
e: Richard Arkwright improved the carding machine, which prepared fibres for spinning, and developed horse-driven spinning mills that used only one machine, which increased efficiency and production. He later used steam engines.

t: What caused the Irish famine of the mid-1800s?
e: In the mid-1840s the potato crop failed in Ireland, and Irish people relied heavily on potatoes for food. A million people died from disease and starvation, and a further 1.5 million left Ireland.

t: In which year was Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, born?
e: Dolly the sheep was the first mammal to be cloned from an adult cell, in 1996. The work was carried out by a team at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh.

t: What was built to link factories to towns, cities and ports during the Industrial Revolution?
e: Better transport links were needed to carry raw materials and manufactured goods. Canals were built to link factories to towns and cities and to the ports, particularly in the middle and north of England.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Boudicca was queen of the Iceni.
e: Boudicca was the queen of the Iceni, a tribe in what is now eastern England, and fought against the Romans. There is a statue of her on Westminster Bridge.

t: In which year was the National Health Service established?
e: The National Health Service (NHS) began in 1948 under the post-war Labour government. It guaranteed a minimum standard of healthcare for all, free at the point of use.

t: Missionaries led by St Augustine came from where?
e: St Augustine led missionaries from Rome who spread Christianity in the south of England. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

t: Roughly how long did the Romans stay in Britain?
e: The Romans arrived successfully in AD 43 and left in AD 410 to defend other parts of their empire, so they stayed for about 400 years. During this time they built roads and public buildings, created a legal structure and introduced new plants and animals.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Hadrian's Wall was built to keep out the Picts.
Hadrian's Wall was built to keep out the Vikings.
e: The Roman Emperor Hadrian had a wall built in the north of England to keep out the Picts, the ancestors of the Scottish people. The Vikings came much later.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: In 1918, women over 30 were given the right to vote.
In 1918, women over 18 were given the right to vote.
e: In 1918, women over the age of 30 were given the right to vote. In 1928 the voting age for women was lowered to 21, the same as men.

t: Which TWO social measures were introduced before the First World War?
e: Before the First World War, Britain introduced a number of social reforms, including free school meals, old-age pensions and support for people who were unemployed. The NHS and free secondary education came after the Second World War.

t: In the Middle Ages, people came to England with special skills. Where did the glass manufacturers come from?
e: In the Middle Ages, people came to England from abroad with special skills: weavers from France, engineers from Germany, glass manufacturers from Italy and canal builders from Holland.

t: Until when did the British Empire continue to grow?
e: The British Empire continued to grow until the 1920s. After the Second World War, many countries gained independence and the Empire gradually became the Commonwealth.

t: In 1847, the working hours of women and children were limited to how many hours a day?
e: Working conditions improved in the 19th century. In 1847 the number of hours that women and children could work was limited by law to 10 hours per day.

t: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII and which wife?
e: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII and his second wife, Anne Boleyn. She was a Protestant who re-established the Church of England, and she became one of the most popular monarchs in English history.

t: Sir Bernard Lovell built a radio telescope at which place?
e: Research into radar led to the development of radio astronomy. Sir Bernard Lovell built a radio telescope at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire, which was for many years the biggest in the world.

t: Which architect designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire?
e: After the Great Fire of London in 1666, Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral and many other churches. St Paul's is still a famous feature of the London skyline.

t: What was the Easter Rising of 1916?
o: An uprising in Dublin against the British
e: In 1916 there was an uprising, the Easter Rising, against the British in Dublin. Its leaders were executed under military law, and a guerrilla war followed, leading to the partition of Ireland in 1922.

t: Where did Isaac Newton study?
e: Isaac Newton was born in Lincolnshire and went on to study at Trinity College, Cambridge. He became an important figure in the scientific revolution.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.
Inigo Jones designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.
e: Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of 1666. Inigo Jones designed the Queen's House at Greenwich.

t: When did the BBC begin the world's first regular television service?
e: The BBC started radio broadcasts in 1922 and began the world's first regular television service in 1936.

t: In 1990, Britain helped liberate which country after it was invaded by Iraq?
e: In 1990, Britain was involved in the international coalition that liberated Kuwait after it was invaded by Iraq. Later, in 2003, British forces took part in the invasion of Iraq.

t: Who became Prime Minister after Labour won the 1945 election?
e: The Labour Party won the 1945 general election, and Clement Attlee became Prime Minister. His government created the NHS and nationalised major industries.

t: Which TWO facts are true about Clement Attlee?
o: He was Churchill's Deputy Prime Minister in the wartime coalition
He led the Labour Party for 20 years
He was Prime Minister from 1960 to 1970
e: Clement Attlee was Churchill's Deputy Prime Minister in the wartime coalition government and led the Labour Party for 20 years. He was Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951.

t: True or false? Elizabeth I asked people about their real religious beliefs and punished those who disagreed.
e: Elizabeth I did not ask about people's real beliefs. She succeeded in finding a balance between the views of Catholics and more extreme Protestants, which helped avoid serious religious conflict in England during her reign.

t: In which year was there a revolution in France?
e: There was a revolution in France in 1789, and the new French government soon declared war on Britain. The wars with Napoleon ended with his defeat at Waterloo in 1815.

t: How long did Queen Victoria reign?
e: Queen Victoria came to the throne in 1837 aged 18 and reigned until 1901, almost 64 years. Her reign was the longest of any monarch at that time, and is known as the Victorian period.

t: Before becoming an MP, Churchill was which TWO things?
e: Before becoming an MP, Winston Churchill was a soldier and a journalist. He became a Conservative MP in 1900.

t: Rudyard Kipling won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907. Which book did he write?
e: Rudyard Kipling, born in India in 1865, wrote books and poems set in India and the UK, including The Jungle Book and the poem 'If'. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

t: Roughly how many casualties did the British suffer on the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916?
e: The handbook says the British suffered 60,000 casualties on the first day of the Battle of the Somme, 1 July 1916, making it one of the bloodiest battles of the First World War.

t: In which year was there a major outbreak of plague in London?
e: In 1665 there was a major outbreak of plague in London, and thousands of people died, especially in poorer areas. A year later, in 1666, the Great Fire of London destroyed much of the city.

t: Which TWO kings believed in the "Divine Right of Kings"?
e: James I and his son Charles I believed in the 'Divine Right of Kings', the idea that the king was directly appointed by God to rule. This led to conflict with Parliament and, eventually, the English Civil War.

t: Sake Dean Mahomet opened the first curry house in Britain in 1810. What was it called?
e: Sake Dean Mahomet came to Britain from India and in 1810 opened the Hindoostane Coffee House in George Street, London, the first curry house in Britain. He also introduced 'shampooing' (Indian head massage) to Britain.

t: What language did the Norman ruling class speak?
e: After the Norman Conquest, the king and his noblemen spoke Norman French, while peasants continued to speak Anglo-Saxon. Over time the two languages combined to become English.

t: By about which year were Anglo-Saxon kingdoms established in Britain?
e: The languages of the Jutes, Angles and Saxons are the basis of modern-day English. By about AD 600, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were established in Britain, mainly in what is now England.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Adam Smith developed ideas about economics.
Adam Smith invented the steam engine.
e: Adam Smith was a thinker of the Scottish Enlightenment who developed ideas about economics that are still referred to today. James Watt worked on steam power.

t: What does the cross of St Patrick look like?
o: A red diagonal cross on a white ground
A red cross on a white ground
A white diagonal cross on a blue ground
A green cross on a white ground
e: The cross of St Patrick, patron saint of Ireland, is a red diagonal cross on a white ground. It was added to the Union Flag in 1801.

t: Which TWO writers were prominent in the inter-war period?
e: The inter-war period saw many developments in the arts and literature. Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh were prominent writers of this time. Dickens and Austen wrote in the 19th century.

t: When did Winston Churchill become Prime Minister?
e: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in May 1940, after Germany invaded Belgium, the Netherlands and France. He led Britain through the war and refused to surrender.

t: Under the Bill of Rights, how often did a new Parliament have to be elected?
e: The Bill of Rights stated that a new Parliament had to be elected at least every three years. This later became every seven years, and it is now at least every five years.

t: Mount Stewart garden is in which part of the UK?
e: Mount Stewart is in Northern Ireland. Other famous gardens include Kew, Sissinghurst and Hidcote (England), Crathes Castle and Inveraray Castle (Scotland) and Bodnant Garden (Wales).

t: What kind of church is the Church of Scotland?
o: A Presbyterian church, governed by ministers and elders
A branch of the Church of England
A Catholic church led by the Pope
The established church for the whole UK
e: The Church of Scotland is the national church of Scotland and is a Presbyterian church. It is governed by ministers and elders, and its chairperson is the Moderator, who is appointed for one year only.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Football is the UK's most popular sport.
Cricket is the UK's most popular sport.
e: Football is the UK's most popular sport. Cricket is also popular, but is not the most popular.

t: When are pubs usually open during the day?
e: Pubs are usually open during the day from 11.00 am (12 noon on Sundays). Night clubs usually open and close later.

t: How are most UK TV channels other than the BBC funded?
e: The BBC is paid for by TV licences. Other UK channels are primarily funded through advertisements and subscriptions.

t: Where is the Wimbledon Championships held?
o: The All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club
e: The Wimbledon Championships is held at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club in London. It is the oldest tennis tournament in the world and the only 'Grand Slam' event played on grass.

t: Who developed new treatments for spinal injuries and founded what became the Paralympics?
e: The Paralympic Games have their origins in the work of Dr Sir Ludwig Guttmann, a German refugee, at Stoke Mandeville hospital. He developed new methods of treatment for people with spinal injuries and encouraged them to take part in exercise and sport.

t: When is Father's Day?
e: Father's Day is the third Sunday in June. Children send cards or buy gifts for their fathers.

t: Who first built the Tower of London?
e: William the Conqueror first built the Tower of London after he became king in 1066. It has since been used as a palace and a prison.

t: Which TWO are medieval cathedrals given as examples in the handbook?
e: In the Middle Ages, great cathedrals such as those in Durham, Lincoln, Canterbury and Salisbury were built. Coventry and Liverpool cathedrals are much more modern.

t: Which TWO musicals did Andrew Lloyd Webber write with Tim Rice?
e: Andrew Lloyd Webber has written the music for shows that have been popular throughout the world, including Jesus Christ Superstar and Evita, in collaboration with Tim Rice, and later Cats and The Phantom of the Opera.

t: What was the UK population in 1901?
e: The UK population grew fast in the 19th century. It was 8 million in 1801, 20 million in 1851 and 40 million in 1901.

t: Which comedy show, first broadcast in 1969, introduced a new type of progressive comedy?
o: That Was The Week That Was
e: Monty Python's Flying Circus, first broadcast in 1969, introduced a new type of progressive comedy. It is still admired today, and satire and comedy are a big part of British culture.

t: In which county is Stoke Mandeville hospital?
e: Stoke Mandeville hospital, where the Paralympics began through the work of Dr Sir Ludwig Guttmann, is in Buckinghamshire.

t: In 2010, the UK population was...
e: In 2010 the UK population was just over 62 million. Population growth has been faster in recent years, partly because of migration and longer life expectancy.

t: Which of these galleries is NOT in London?
e: The National Gallery of Scotland is in Edinburgh, not London. Tate Modern, Tate Britain and the National Gallery are all in London.

t: What did Thomas Chippendale design?
e: Thomas Chippendale designed furniture in the 18th century. Other British designers include Clarice Cliff (art deco ceramics) and Mary Quant (fashion).

t: True or false? Shops and businesses must accept Scottish and Northern Irish banknotes.
e: Northern Ireland and Scotland have their own banknotes, which are valid everywhere in the UK. However, shops and businesses do not have to accept them.

t: What can people see at the Tower of London?
e: The Tower of London was first built by William the Conqueror. Visitors can see the Crown Jewels there, and tours are given by the Yeoman Warders (Beefeaters).

t: Which TWO describe Handel?
o: He was German-born and became a British citizen
He wrote Music for the Royal Fireworks
He was organist at Westminster Abbey
e: George Frederick Handel was German-born and spent many years in the UK, becoming a British citizen in 1727. He wrote the Water Music for George I and Music for the Royal Fireworks for George II.

t: Which flower is associated with England?
e: The rose is associated with England. The other national flowers are the thistle (Scotland), the daffodil (Wales) and the shamrock (Northern Ireland).

t: Where did Great Britain finish in the 2012 Olympic medal table?
e: The 2012 Olympic Games were held in London, and Great Britain came third in the medal table, winning 29 gold medals.

t: Which TWO painters from abroad worked in Britain in the 16th and 17th centuries?
e: In the 16th and 17th centuries, most of the artists working in Britain came from abroad, for example Hans Holbein and Sir Anthony Van Dyck. Turner and Constable were British painters of the 18th and 19th centuries.

t: Which TWO cities are in Scotland?
e: Dundee and Aberdeen are cities in Scotland, along with Edinburgh, Glasgow and Inverness. Newport is in Wales and Norwich is in England.

t: Roughly what share of the UK population lives in Northern Ireland?
e: Northern Ireland makes up less than 3% of the UK's population. England has about 84%, Scotland just over 8% and Wales around 5%.

t: What is the most common ethnic description chosen in UK surveys?
e: The UK population is ethnically diverse and changing rapidly, especially in large cities. Most people choose 'White' as their ethnic description, and many others choose Asian, Black or mixed.

t: Which artist is considered to have raised the profile of landscape painting?
e: Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775–1851) was an influential landscape painter in a modern style. He is considered the artist who raised the profile of landscape painting. The Turner Prize is named after him.

t: Which architect designed the Cenotaph in Whitehall?
e: Sir Edwin Lutyens designed the Cenotaph in Whitehall, which is the site of the annual Remembrance Day service. He had a great influence on buildings in New Delhi, India.

t: How many national parks are there in England, Wales and Scotland?
e: There are 15 national parks in England, Wales and Scotland. They are areas of protected countryside that everyone can visit, where people live, work and look after the landscape.

t: In which county is the Eden Project?
e: The Eden Project is in Cornwall, in the south-west of England. Its giant greenhouses (biomes) house plants from all over the world, and it is also an educational charity.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The BBC is funded by money from TV licences.
The BBC is funded by advertising.
e: The BBC is funded by money from TV licences and does not show advertisements. Other channels are funded by advertising and subscriptions.

t: True or false? More women than men study at university in the UK.
e: On average, girls leave school with better qualifications than boys, and more women than men study at university. Women work in all sectors of the economy.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Sir Roger Bannister was the first man to run a mile in under four minutes.
Sir Roger Bannister was the first Briton to win the Tour de France.
e: Sir Roger Bannister was the first man to run a mile in under four minutes, in 1954. The first Briton to win the Tour de France was Bradley Wiggins, in 2012.

t: What are Welsh cakes?
o: A snack made from flour, dried fruits and spices
A sheep's stomach stuffed with oatmeal
e: Welsh cakes are a traditional Welsh snack made from flour, dried fruits and spices, and served either hot or cold. The other options describe haggis (Scotland), Ulster fry (Northern Ireland) and Yorkshire pudding (England).

t: What is sent to you before an election, telling you where to vote?
e: Before an election, you will be sent a poll card telling you where your polling station is and when the election will take place.

t: Which TWO are key roles of school governors?
o: Setting the strategic direction of the school
e: School governors are people from the local community who wish to make a positive contribution to children's education. Their key roles are setting the strategic direction of the school, ensuring accountability, and monitoring and evaluating school performance.

t: In Scotland, what third verdict is possible besides "guilty" and "not guilty"?
e: In Scotland there are three possible verdicts: 'guilty', 'not guilty' or 'not proven'. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, a jury can only find the defendant 'guilty' or 'not guilty'.

t: Which TWO are benefits of volunteering mentioned in the handbook?
o: A chance to practise your English
Developing work skills for your CV
e: Volunteering helps others and gives you a chance to practise your English, develop work skills for your CV and meet new people. It is unpaid work.

t: In which decades did the Chartists campaign for reform?
e: The Chartists campaigned for reform in the 1830s and 1840s. They wanted every man to have the vote, elections every year, equal-sized electoral districts, secret ballots, any man to be able to stand as an MP, and MPs to be paid.

t: Which TWO of these are civil law matters?
o: A dispute between a landlord and tenant over repairs
e: Civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups, such as housing disputes between landlords and tenants and employment issues like unfair dismissal. Selling alcohol to under-18s and carrying a knife are criminal offences.

t: True or false? The Council of Europe can make laws for its members.
e: The Council of Europe has no power to make laws, but it does draw up conventions and charters, which focus on human rights, democracy, education, the environment, health and culture.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Polling stations are open from 7.00 am until 10.00 pm.
Polling stations are open from 9.00 am until 5.00 pm.
e: Polling stations are open from 7.00 am until 10.00 pm on election day.

t: Which TWO are roles of the monarch in representing the UK?
o: Receiving foreign ambassadors and high commissioners
e: The monarch represents the UK to the rest of the world. They receive foreign ambassadors and high commissioners, entertain visiting heads of state, and make state visits overseas in support of diplomatic and economic relationships. Foreign policy is decided by the government.

t: Which of these statements about the Speaker is NOT true?
o: The Speaker is chosen by the monarch
The Speaker is chosen by MPs in a secret ballot
The Speaker keeps order during debates
e: The Speaker is chosen by MPs in a secret ballot, not by the monarch. The Speaker is politically neutral and keeps order during debates.

t: True or false? Each devolved administration has its own civil service.
e: Each devolved administration (in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland) has its own civil service to support it.

t: Which TWO services are paid for by income tax?
e: Money raised from income tax pays for government services such as roads, education, the police and the armed forces. Private schools and supermarkets are not funded this way.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
The Human Rights Act was agreed by King John in 1215.
e: The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. Magna Carta was agreed by King John in 1215.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: MPs are elected through a system called 'first past the post'.
MPs are elected through proportional representation.
e: MPs are elected through the 'first past the post' system: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins. European Parliament elections used proportional representation.

t: What can living people donate, besides blood?
e: Many people in the UK need organ transplants. You can register to donate your organs when you die. Living people can also donate a kidney.

t: What can you do if it is difficult for you to get to a polling station?
o: Ask a friend to vote without registering
e: If it is difficult for you to get to a polling station, you can register for a postal ballot. Your ballot paper will be sent to your home before the election, and you post it back.

t: Which TWO are core values of the Commonwealth?
e: The Commonwealth is based on the core values of democracy, good government and the rule of law. It has no power over its members, has no shared currency and no common army.

t: True or false? A man who forces his wife to have sex can be charged with rape.
e: Any man who forces a woman to have sex, including a man who forces his wife, can be charged with rape. Domestic violence in any form is a crime.

t: True or false? Members of the House of Lords represent a constituency.
e: Members of the House of Lords (peers) are not elected by the people and do not represent a constituency. MPs in the House of Commons each represent a constituency.

t: Which TWO kinds of member sit in the House of Lords?
o: Senior bishops of the Church of England
e: The House of Lords includes life peers (appointed for their lifetime, often after distinguished careers), some hereditary peers, and senior bishops of the Church of England. Members of the Lords are not elected by the people.

t: The UK is one of how many permanent members of the UN Security Council?
e: The UK is one of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, which recommends action when there are international crises and threats to peace. The UN was set up after the Second World War.

t: In Scotland, serious civil cases are dealt with in which court?
o: The Court of Session in Edinburgh
e: In Scotland, most civil cases are heard in the Sheriff Court, and more serious civil cases are dealt with in the Court of Session in Edinburgh.

t: True or false? The Speaker of the House of Commons is chosen by the Prime Minister.
e: The Speaker of the House of Commons is chosen by other MPs in a secret ballot, not by the Prime Minister.

t: How many countries are members of the United Nations?
e: The UK is part of the United Nations (UN), an international organisation with more than 190 countries as members. It was set up after the Second World War to prevent war and promote international peace and security.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: In Scotland a jury has 15 members.
In Scotland a jury has 12 members.
e: In Scotland a jury has 15 members. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland a jury has 12 members.

t: Which charity works with animals?
e: The PDSA (People's Dispensary for Sick Animals) is a charity that works with animals. It helps treat animals whose owners cannot afford a vet.
